stem: A 24-year-old patient presents with a 1-week history of recurrent painful oral ulcers. The lesions are shallow, round-to-oval, and located on the non-keratinized oral mucosa (buccal mucosa and inner lips). There is no history of vesicular eruption, no fever, no genital lesions, no skin rash, and no systemic symptoms. Examination reveals no lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Early squamous cell carcinoma of oral mucosa
keywords: “Recurrent painful oral ulcers” → strongly suggests aphthous spectrum disorder rather than infection or malignancy
“Non-keratinized mucosa (buccal mucosa, inner lips)” → classic site for aphthous ulcers
“No vesicles, no fever, no systemic symptoms” → excludes HSV, Behçet, systemic inflammatory disease

C.title: Recurrent Aphthous Stomatitis
C.body:
Recurrent aphthous stomatitis is a common idiopathic condition characterized by recurrent, shallow, painful ulcers on non-keratinized oral mucosa. It typically occurs in young adults and has no systemic involvement. Lesions are round or oval with a yellow-gray base and erythematous halo. It is strongly associated with stress, minor trauma, or nutritional deficiencies.
In this patient, the absence of vesicles, systemic symptoms, and localization to buccal mucosa strongly supports aphthous stomatitis as the primary diagnosis.
C.clinicalReasoning: This is the classic presentation of minor recurrent aphthous ulcers. The lesions are shallow, recurrent, and confined to non-keratinized mucosa without systemic features. HSV is unlikely due to absence of vesicles, and lichen planus or malignancy would have chronic or indurated features. This is the most common cause of recurrent painful oral ulcers in healthy young adults.

A.title: Herpetiform Aphthous Ulceration
A.body: This is a variant of aphthous stomatitis characterized by multiple small clustered ulcers resembling herpes infection but without viral etiology. It occurs on non-keratinized mucosa and is extremely painful. Unlike HSV, there are no vesicles or systemic prodrome. It is less common than recurrent aphthous stomatitis.
A.clinicalReasoning: Although similar in location and pain pattern, herpetiform aphthous ulcers typically present as numerous pinpoint lesions rather than typical round/oval ulcers described here. The stem does not mention clustered lesions, making this less likely than classic aphthous stomatitis.

B.title: Traumatic Ulceration
B.body: Traumatic ulcers result from mechanical injury such as biting, sharp teeth, or dental appliances. They are usually solitary, irregular, and directly related to a clear local cause. Healing occurs after removal of irritant.
B.clinicalReasoning: No history of trauma or localized mechanical irritation is given. Additionally, recurrence over time without trigger is not typical. The bilateral mucosal involvement and recurrence pattern argue against trauma.

D.title: Erosive Oral Lichen Planus
D.body: This is a chronic immune-mediated condition characterized by white lacy striations (Wickham striae) with erosive, painful ulcerations. It is often persistent and may involve skin or other mucosa.
D.clinicalReasoning: The absence of white reticular lesions, chronic course, and systemic mucocutaneous involvement makes this unlikely. Lichen planus is typically chronic and not purely episodic recurrent ulcers.

E.title: Early Squamous Cell Carcinoma of Oral Mucosa
E.body: Oral SCC typically presents as a non-healing indurated ulcer, often in older patients with risk factors like tobacco or alcohol use. Lesions are persistent and may bleed or become exophytic.
E.clinicalReasoning: Age is inappropriate (young patient), and lesions are recurrent and painful rather than persistent indurated ulcers. SCC is not episodic and does not resolve spontaneously, making this incorrect.

keyConcept: Recurrent painful oral ulcers in a young healthy adult without systemic features and located on non-keratinized mucosa are most consistent with recurrent aphthous stomatitis. Absence of vesicles excludes HSV, while lack of chronic induration excludes malignancy. Localization and recurrence pattern are the strongest diagnostic clues.
